nama_domain: Smart Manufacturing & Industry 4.0 (industrial robotics, lights-out/'dark' factories, AI-driven production, and the transition into embodied AI / humanoid factory labor)
kategori: Industri & Energi (Industry & Energy) — with deep spillovers into Ketenagakerjaan (labor displacement of factory workers), Pendidikan Vokasi (vocational/engineering education), and Kebijakan Industri (industrial policy and FDI strategy)
tahun_mulai_china: Three distinct waves. (1) ROBOTIZATION wave: 2013 — the year China became the world's largest industrial robot market by annual installations, driven by rising coastal wages after the 2010 Foxconn suicides and the Pearl River Delta labor shortage. Codified as state policy on 19 May 2015 with 'Made in China 2025' (中国制造2025) and the 'Robot Industry Development Plan 2016-2020'. (2) SMART/DARK FACTORY wave: 2019-2021 — MIIT's smart manufacturing standards program plus 5G+industrial internet; Xiaomi's fully automated Changping smart factory and Foxconn/BYD/CATL lights-out lines became the showcase; formalized in 2025 as the six-ministry 'Smart Factory Gradient Cultivation Action' (智能工厂梯度培育行动). (3) EMBODIED AI / HUMANOID wave: 2023-2025 — MIIT's Humanoid Robot Innovation Guidance (Nov 2023) set 2025 mass-production and 2027 world-leading targets; 2025 was declared the 'year one of embodied AI commercialization'; embodied intelligence (具身智能) was written into the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) as a national 'future industry' alongside quantum tech and brain-computer interfaces.
pemain_kunci_china: ROBOT MAKERS & INTEGRATORS: Estun (埃斯顿), Siasun (新松), Efort (埃夫特), Inovance (汇川技术 — now the largest domestic supplier by units), JAKA, Rokae, Dobot, plus foreign incumbents losing share (Fanuc, ABB, Yaskawa, KUKA — KUKA itself Chinese-owned via Midea since 2016). SMART-FACTORY OPERATORS: Xiaomi (Changping 'dark factory' + Beijing EV plant), Foxconn/Hon Hai (Kunshan, Zhengzhou), BYD, CATL (Ningde 'lighthouse' plants), Haier COSMOPlat, Midea, Gree, Sany Heavy Industry ('Lighthouse Factory' for excavators), Geely, Li Auto, NIO. HUMANOID / EMBODIED AI: Unitree Robotics (宇树, Hangzhou — STAR Market IPO 2026, raised >RMB 4.2 billion), AgiBot/Zhiyuan Robotics (智元机器人, Shanghai), UBTech (优必选, Shenzhen — first to deploy humanoids in auto plants: BYD, Foxconn, Zeekr, Audi-FAW), Unitree's rivals Galbot, Fourier Intelligence, Leju, Xpeng Robotics (IRON), Xiaomi CyberOne, plus 60+ humanoid OEMs and 140+ companies overall. PLATFORM/AI LAYER: Huawei (Ascend chips + Pangu industrial models), Alibaba Cloud, Baidu, DeepSeek (whose cheap open models made factory-floor AI deployment economically viable from early 2025). STATE ACTORS: MIIT (工信部), NDRC, SASAC (which orders central SOEs to deploy humanoids), and provincial funds in Guangdong, Zhejiang, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Anhui.
apa_yang_terjadi_di_china: China has executed the largest and fastest factory automation program in industrial history, and is now attempting a second, more radical leap from fixed automation to general-purpose embodied AI. MECHANISM: (a) Wage-push trigger — coastal manufacturing wages roughly quintupled between 2005 and 2015, destroying the cheap-labor model exactly as the working-age population peaked in 2011-2013; automation became a survival requirement, not an efficiency luxury. (b) State-directed capital — Made in China 2025 (2015), the Robot+ Application Action Plan (Jan 2023), and the Smart Factory Gradient Cultivation Action (2025) combined subsidies, tax credits, procurement mandates on SOEs, and local-government equipment-renewal funds; provinces competed to hit robot-installation KPIs. (c) Vertical integration of the robot supply chain — China deliberately localized the three chokepoint components (reducers, servo motors, controllers), historically dominated by Nabtesco, Harmonic Drive and Yaskawa; domestic brands crossed 50% of the home market in 2024 and China became a NET EXPORTER of industrial robots in 2025. (d) Full-stack 'dark factory' architecture — Xiaomi's Changping plant runs on its in-house HyperIMP platform where machines self-schedule, self-diagnose and self-optimize with no humans on the production floor and no lighting or HVAC needed, producing roughly one smartphone per second. Foxconn, BYD, CATL and Midea have replicated lights-out lines across dozens of sites. (e) Embodied AI transition — from 2025, humanoid and wheeled-humanoid robots began entering real production environments (UBTech Walker S series at BYD, Foxconn, Zeekr and Audi-FAW; AgiBot and Unitree units in logistics, inspection and assembly), targeting the ~40-60% of factory tasks that fixed automation cannot economically address because they require dexterity, adaptation, or work in human-designed spaces. In 2026 MIIT and SASAC launched a joint 'real-world training' campaign to force commercialization of 10,000 humanoids across 100+ high-value scenarios by year end. IMPACT: China now produces roughly 30% of global manufacturing value added and drove over 30% of global manufacturing growth in 2021-2025, while its manufacturing workforce shrank by more than 30 million people — output and employment have fully decoupled. The strategic logic is explicit: use robots to keep manufacturing onshore despite demographic decline, tariffs, and wage convergence, and to export the automation stack itself as the next big-ticket industry after solar, batteries and EVs.
data_skala_china: ROBOT INSTALLATIONS & STOCK: 295,000 industrial robots installed in 2024 = 54% of the global total of 542,000 units (IFR World Robotics 2025); operational stock ~2 million units, the world's largest and about 4.5x Japan in second place; China has installed more robots annually than the rest of the world combined since 2021. ROBOT DENSITY: 166 robots per 10,000 manufacturing employees in 2024 per IFR World Robotics 2025 (a sharp downward restatement from the previously published 470 figure, caused by China's National Bureau of Statistics revising manufacturing employment upward) — versus South Korea 1,220, Singapore 818, Germany 449, Japan 446, USA 307; China ranks around 22nd globally on density despite being #1 in absolute stock, meaning enormous headroom remains. ROBOT PRODUCTION: 556,400 industrial robots produced in 2024 (+14.2% YoY); over 770,000 units in 2025 (+28% YoY); robot exports grew 48.7% in 2025 and exceeded imports for the first time; Chinese shipments of ~330,000 units in 2025 were ~56% of the global 570,000, more than the US, Germany, Japan and Korea combined. INDUSTRY VALUE: China's industrial robot industry reached RMB 247.5 billion in 2025 (+27.8%), split into RMB 108 billion for robot bodies and RMB 139.5 billion for system integration; domestic brands took 52.45% market share in 2024, the first time above half; smart equipment manufacturing revenue grew 28.1% in 2025, with special-operation robot manufacturing up 42.1%. SMART FACTORIES: cumulative MIIT-recognized totals as of 2025-2026 — over 35,000 basic-level (基础级), over 8,200 advanced-level (先进级), over 500 excellence-level (卓越级), and the first batch of 15 leading-level (领航级) smart factories announced at end-2025. HUMANOIDS: 2025 global humanoid shipments were 85-90% Chinese, led by Unitree ~5,500 units and AgiBot ~5,168 units; AgiBot rolled out its 10,000th general-purpose embodied robot (Expedition A3) in late March 2026 after scaling 1,000 → 5,000 → 10,000 units within three months; Unitree targets 20,000 shipments in 2026 with announced capacity for 75,000 humanoids and 115,000 quadrupeds per year; TrendForce projects Chinese humanoid output to rise 94% in 2026 with Unitree + AgiBot taking ~80% share; the MIIT/SASAC target is 10,000 commercially deployed humanoids and 100+ validated scenarios by end-2026; the sector already has 140+ companies and 330+ products. EMPLOYMENT: manufacturing employment fell from roughly 115 million in 2013 to under 85 million in 2025 — a loss of 30+ million jobs while output and exports hit records; PwC estimates ~26% of Chinese jobs (~204 million) are exposed to automation over two decades. SHOWCASE ECONOMICS: Xiaomi's Changping dark factory cost ~RMB 2.4 billion (~US$330 million) for 81,000 m² and ~10 million handsets per year with zero floor workers; Foxconn's Kunshan plant cut over 60,000 jobs through robotization.
fase_tren_di_china: Two-speed. (1) Industrial robotics / smart factories = MATURE-TO-CONSOLIDATING: penetration is deep, domestic supply chains are localized, growth has shifted from installation volume to density deepening, export competition, and margin compression. Price wars among Chinese robot arm makers are now severe, and the sector shows classic 'involution' (内卷) symptoms — volume up, profits down. (2) Embodied AI / humanoid robots = BOOMING / EARLY-BUBBLE: 2025 was 'year one of commercialization', 2026 is the declared inflection from novelty to routine deployment, with state procurement targets, a new MIIT standardization committee (Dec 2025), the first Humanoid Robotics and Embodied Intelligence Standard System (Feb 2026), and record IPO valuations. Simultaneously the first bubble warnings have appeared: Caixin reported in June 2026 that founders and investors fear the sector will replicate the EV industry's self-destructive price war, with 60+ humanoid OEMs and rapid price collapse in semi-humanoid and entertainment segments. Meanwhile a third phase is emerging — REGULATED/BACKLASH on the labor side: MOHRSS announced on 27 January 2026 that China will issue a dedicated policy document on responding to AI's employment impact, signaling that Beijing now treats automation-driven displacement as a governance problem, not just an industrial win.
puncak_tren_china: Industrial robot INSTALLATION peak (as a share of global demand and as a growth story): 2023-2025, concentrated in the Yangtze River Delta (Suzhou, Ningbo, Shanghai), Pearl River Delta (Shenzhen, Dongguan, Foshan), and Chongqing/Chengdu, in three sectors — electronics/3C, automotive & EV, and lithium batteries. Peak PRODUCTION year so far: 2025 (770,000+ units, +28%, first year as net exporter). Smart-factory policy peak: 2025-2026, when the gradient-cultivation program named its first 15 'leading-level' factories. Embodied AI/humanoid peak is NOT yet reached — the hype peak is likely 2026-2027 (shipment growth of ~94% in 2026, mass IPOs, state deployment campaign), with a probable shakeout and consolidation in 2028-2030 leaving a handful of survivors, mirroring the EV sector's 2018-2019 hype peak and 2023-2025 consolidation.
status_di_indonesia: Baru mulai / partial and enclaved (early stage, concentrated in enclaves). Industrial robotics exists in Indonesia but only inside a narrow band of foreign-owned, export-oriented, capital-intensive plants — automotive assembly (Toyota, Daihatsu, Hyundai, Wuling, BYD), electronics/EMS, and to a lesser degree food & beverage, pharma and mining processing. There is essentially NO lights-out/dark factory, no domestic robot manufacturing industry of consequence, and humanoid/embodied AI is at the demonstration-and-inspection-pilot stage only. Simultaneously Indonesia is experiencing PREMATURE DEINDUSTRIALIZATION — manufacturing is roughly 19% of GDP versus a ~32% peak in 2002 — so the country is losing labor-intensive factory jobs to competitiveness and import pressure BEFORE automation is even the main cause. This is the crucial asymmetry: China automated from a position of manufacturing dominance and labor scarcity; Indonesia faces automation from a position of industrial weakness and labor surplus.
contoh_konkret_indonesia: AUTOMOTIVE (the deepest adopter): PT Hyundai Motor Manufacturing Indonesia (Cikarang, Bekasi) runs Hyundai-built robots across stamping, welding, and quality control lines; Toyota Motor Manufacturing Indonesia and Astra Daihatsu Motor (Karawang, Sunter) use robotic welding and painting cells; Wuling/SGMW (Cikarang) has publicly stated it will progressively convert its Indonesian plant to the I2MS smart-factory architecture used in Liuzhou, where autonomous mobile robots replace fixed conveyor rails — SGMW Vice President Han Dehong framed it as 'step by step, we will modify the Jakarta plant into I2MS'; PT BYD Motor Indonesia's US$1 billion, 150,000-unit/year plant at Subang Smartpolitan (108+ hectares) completed construction end-2025 and began operating in 2026 producing the M6 and Atto 1 — it arrives with a modern, heavily robotized body shop by design, making it the single most automated greenfield plant Indonesia has received. ELECTRONICS: contract assembly in Batam and Cikarang (Sat Nusapersada and similar EMS firms) uses SMT lines and pick-and-place automation but remains manual at final assembly, packing and QC — the opposite of Xiaomi's dark factory. HUMANOID/EMBODIED AI: Halo Robotics (Jakarta, est. 2014) is the sole official Unitree distributor and after-sales service center in Indonesia, serving 900+ corporate and government clients; as of 2026 it reports humanoid robots entering trials in Indonesian manufacturing environments for repetitive visual inspection and facility documentation, and quadruped robots (Unitree Go/B series) doing routine inspection with gas sensors and cameras in mining, oil & gas and manufacturing — explicitly framed as taking over monotonous tasks rather than replacing operators. POLICY: 'Making Indonesia 4.0' launched by President Jokowi on 4 April 2018 with seven priority sectors and a target of raising manufacturing to 25% of GDP by 2030; the INDI 4.0 readiness index (five pillars, 17 assessment fields) run by Kemenperin, with awareness workshops extended down to IKM/SME level. FDI CHANNEL: November 2025 saw 16 Indonesia-China industrial cooperation MoUs worth IDR 36.4 trillion covering metals, textiles, batteries, drones and AI; China was Indonesia's third-largest FDI source in Q1 2026 at US$2.2 billion; Hisense signed a strategic cooperation MoU with Danantara in Jakarta in May 2026; TCL is exploring commercial AC production locally.
data_skala_indonesia: MANUFACTURING BASE: manufacturing value added ~US$255 billion, roughly 12th in the world (World Bank, 2023 basis), but only ~1.5% of global MVA versus China's ~30% — an approximately 20:1 gap. Manufacturing is 18.98% of GDP (2024), down from a ~32% peak in 2002. Non-oil-and-gas manufacturing grew 5.30% in 2025, above national GDP growth of 5.11% — the first time in over a decade. WORKFORCE: roughly 20.3 million manufacturing workers as of August 2025 (13.86% of 146.5 million employed), up ~0.30 million YoY — i.e. Indonesia is still ADDING factory workers while China sheds them. ROBOT ADOPTION: Indonesia's robotics market is estimated at only ~US$23.8 million in 2025, projected to reach ~US$47.75 million by 2030 (CAGR ~14.9%) — three orders of magnitude below China's RMB 247.5 billion (~US$34 billion) industrial robot industry. Historic IFR-referenced installations were ~950 units (2017) and ~1,200 units (2018) versus Thailand ~4,000/year and Vietnam ~3,000/year; Indonesia ranked last in ASEAN for industrial robot adoption in IFR's 2016 assessment and has not published a country density figure since. Estimated current robot density is in the single digits to low teens per 10,000 manufacturing workers, versus China's 166 and Singapore's 818 [uncertain — IFR does not publish a separate Indonesia density line; this is inferred from installation history and the ~20 million worker denominator]. LABOR MARKET STRESS (not primarily automation-driven yet): 60 textile factories closed 2022-2024 affecting ~250,000 workers; Sritex ceased operations 1 March 2025 laying off 10,660+; Kemnaker recorded 42,000+ layoffs January-June 2025 (KSPI claims up to 70,000); Manufacturing PMI fell to 46.7 in April 2025, the steepest contraction since August 2021; labor absorption in labor-intensive sectors fell from 471,972 workers (2024) to 444,110 (2025) and 202,244 in H1 2026 (-7.7% YoY). WAGES: average provincial minimum wage ~IDR 3.32 million/month in 2025 (Jakarta IDR 5,396,760; Central Java IDR 2,169,348) — roughly US$1.85/hour minimum versus China's ~US$3.70/hour, i.e. Indonesian factory labor still costs about half of Chinese minimum-wage labor and a small fraction of Chinese average manufacturing wages. SKILLS: Kemenperin's vocational units produced 5,472 industry-ready graduates in 2025 — a rounding error against a 20-million-worker manufacturing sector.
estimasi_lag_tahun: Not one number — the lag differs sharply by layer. (a) BASIC INDUSTRIAL ROBOTIZATION (welding, painting, palletizing, SMT): Indonesia's current density is roughly where China stood around 2010-2013, implying a lag of 12-15 years. (b) INTEGRATED SMART FACTORY / MES + IoT + digital twin at scale: China's gradient program produced 35,000+ recognized smart factories by 2025; Indonesia has a readiness index and pilot participants but no comparable installed base — lag of 12-18 years. (c) LIGHTS-OUT / DARK FACTORIES: China 2019-2025 at commercial scale; Indonesia effectively zero and unlikely to be economic under current wage structure — lag of 15-25 years, and possibly never in the same form. (d) EMBODIED AI / HUMANOID ROBOTS IN PRODUCTION: China entered commercial deployment 2025-2026; Indonesia is running inspection pilots in 2026 through a single distributor — the TECHNOLOGY lag is small (2-4 years, because hardware is imported and China is exporting aggressively), but the DEPLOYMENT SCALE lag is 10-15 years. Weighted headline estimate: approximately 12-15 years for the automation stack as a whole, but with a compressing frontier layer — Indonesia will get to touch humanoid robots far sooner, relative to China, than it got to touch industrial robot arms. [uncertain — no official Indonesian robot density series exists, so the density-matching method carries a ±4-year error band]
bukti_historical_lag: Three convergent lines of evidence. (1) DENSITY MATCHING: China's robot density passed roughly 15-25 units per 10,000 workers around 2010-2012 and reached its explosive installation phase from 2013; Indonesia's inferred density today sits in that same low band, and its annual installations (roughly 1,000-3,000 units) resemble China's early-2000s volumes — a 12-15 year offset. (2) POLICY LAG: China issued Made in China 2025 in May 2015; Indonesia issued Making Indonesia 4.0 on 4 April 2018 — a 3-year policy lag, but with roughly a decade of implementation lag, since China had already hit its 25%-of-GDP-manufacturing equivalent while Indonesia's manufacturing share KEPT FALLING (19% in 2024 against a 25%-by-2030 target it will almost certainly miss). Policy adoption is fast in Indonesia; policy execution is not. (3) PRIOR-TREND ANALOGUE: the same 10-15 year pattern held for EVs (BYD launched its first plug-in in 2008 and China's EV share passed 50% of new sales in 2024; Indonesian EV sales only became significant from 2023-2025 with Wuling, BYD and Chery entering), for QR-code payments (China 2014-2016 mass adoption, Indonesia QRIS from 2019-2022), and for social commerce/livestream shopping (China 2016-2019, Indonesia 2021-2024) — a consistent 5-8 year lag for CONSUMER-side trends but a consistently LONGER 12-18 year lag for CAPITAL-side industrial trends, because consumer trends transfer via phones and algorithms while industrial trends require capex, skilled technicians, and reliable power. Smart manufacturing is firmly in the capital-side category. (4) COUNTER-EVIDENCE OF ENCLAVE LEAPFROG: the BYD Subang plant, the Wuling I2MS conversion plan, and the Hyundai Cikarang robot lines show that when a foreign OEM builds greenfield, it imports its CURRENT-generation automation, not a 15-year-old generation — so the lag at individual-plant level can be near zero even while the national average lag is 15 years.
tipe_lag: Laggard (dominant), with two qualifications: (a) ENCLAVE LEAPFROG — foreign greenfield plants (BYD Subang, Wuling I2MS, Hyundai Cikarang) import frontier-generation automation directly, so Indonesia's newest plants can be more modern than its 20-year-old ones by a full technological generation, producing extreme intra-national dispersion rather than uniform lag; and (b) POTENTIAL PARTIAL LEAPFROG IN EMBODIED AI — because humanoid robots are being commoditized and export-pushed by Chinese vendors, Indonesia may acquire humanoids at a smaller lag than it acquired industrial arms, skipping some of the fixed-automation build-out. Net: Laggard in diffusion, near-simultaneous in frontier access, with the gap between the two widening into a dual-track industrial economy.
probabilitas_transfer: Tinggi (High) for the technology and equipment arriving; Sedang (Medium) for it diffusing broadly beyond foreign-owned enclaves; Rendah (Low) for full lights-out/dark-factory replication in the Chinese form within the next decade.
alasan_probabilitas: HIGH for arrival because the transfer is being PUSHED rather than pulled. China has become a net exporter of industrial robots (exports +48.7% in 2025) and faces domestic overcapacity and involution-driven price wars, making Southeast Asia a natural dumping and expansion ground; simultaneously US tariffs are pushing Chinese manufacturers to relocate production to Indonesia (China was the third-largest FDI source in Q1 2026 at US$2.2 billion; 16 MoUs worth IDR 36.4 trillion signed in November 2025), and relocated Chinese plants bring Chinese automation standards, Chinese systems integrators, and Chinese equipment financing with them. Falling robot prices — a Chinese six-axis arm now costs a fraction of a Japanese equivalent — steadily lower the wage threshold at which automation pays in Indonesia. MEDIUM for broad diffusion because Indonesia's manufacturing sector is dominated by SMEs and labor-intensive sectors (textiles, footwear, food processing) where minimum wages of ~US$1.85/hour make robot payback periods long, capital is expensive (double-digit lending rates), electricity reliability outside Java is inconsistent, and the technician base to maintain robots is thin — Kemenperin's own vocational pipeline produced only 5,472 industry-ready graduates in 2025. LOW for dark factories because a Chinese lights-out plant requires not just robots but a dense local supplier network, standardized high-volume SKUs, in-house software capability, and stable grid power — Indonesia has none of these at the required density, and its comparative advantage remains cheap labor, which a dark factory explicitly discards.
vektor_transmisi: (a) CHINESE PLAYERS ENTERING DIRECTLY — the dominant vector. BYD's US$1 billion, 150,000-unit Subang plant; Wuling/SGMW's stated plan to convert its Cikarang plant to the I2MS autonomous-mobile-robot architecture; Chery, Aion, Geely and battery/nickel-processing investors in Morowali and Weda Bay; Hisense's May 2026 strategic MoU with Danantara; TCL exploring local AC production. These arrive with their own automation specifications, Chinese systems integrators, Chinese equipment, and often Chinese engineers on secondment. (b) TARIFF-DRIVEN SUPPLY-CHAIN RELOCATION — US tariffs on China are relocating electronics, textile, footwear and automotive component production to Batam/Bintan, Greater Jakarta, Central Java, East Java and Sulawesi; relocated plants are typically MORE automated than the Indonesian incumbents they compete with, because the relocating firm is exporting its Chinese process, not adopting a local one. This is the fastest and least visible vector. (c) EQUIPMENT EXPORT + DISTRIBUTOR NETWORKS — Chinese robot arms, AGVs, AMRs, cobots and now humanoids entering through local distributors; Halo Robotics as sole official Unitree distributor with 900+ clients is the archetype, and Chinese cobot brands (JAKA, Dobot, Elite) compete on price against Fanuc/ABB in Indonesian SME tenders. (d) JAPANESE/KOREAN OEM CHANNEL (non-China but same effect) — Toyota, Daihatsu, Hyundai and Denso have historically been Indonesia's main automation transmission channel and remain the largest installed base; Hyundai Cikarang's Hyundai-built assembly robots are a direct example. (e) LOCAL COPYCAT / SYSTEM INTEGRATION LAYER — Indonesian integrators, engineering consultancies and industrial-IoT startups reselling and adapting Chinese hardware, plus IKM-level 'low-cost automation' retrofits; this is embryonic but is where domestic value capture would have to occur. (f) CHINESE VENTURE AND STATE CAPITAL — funds attached to industrial-park development (Subang Smartpolitan, KIT Batang, Morowali/IMIP) that finance automated greenfield capacity; Danantara as counterparty institutionalizes this. (g) DIASPORA/ALUMNI — Indonesian engineers trained at Chinese universities under BRI scholarships and Indonesian staff of Chinese plants returning with process knowledge; small today but a compounding channel. (h) ALGORITHMIC/CONTENT DIFFUSION — a weak vector for capital goods, but Douyin/TikTok and YouTube footage of Chinese dark factories has already shaped Indonesian elite and public expectations, driving political statements about 'catching up on AI and robotics with China' well ahead of any real capability.
prasyarat_struktural: THRESHOLD CONDITIONS AND INDONESIA'S POSITION VERSUS CHINA AT ITS TAKEOFF. (1) WAGE LEVEL — the single most important trigger. China's robotization exploded from 2013 when coastal manufacturing wages had risen roughly fivefold in a decade and manufacturing labor cost had passed roughly US$3.50-4.50/hour, making a US$25,000-50,000 robot pay back in 2-3 years. Indonesia's average provincial minimum wage is ~IDR 3.32 million/month (~US$1.85/hour, Jakarta ~US$3.00, Central Java ~US$1.20) — i.e. Indonesia today is roughly where China was around 2005-2008 on labor cost. The automation-economics trigger has NOT yet fired for most Indonesian manufacturing; it has already fired for automotive, where cycle-time and quality (not labor cost) drive robotization. (2) LABOR SUPPLY — China automated because it ran OUT of young factory workers (working-age population peaked 2011-2013). Indonesia is the opposite: it is in a demographic bonus until roughly 2035-2040, with 20.3 million manufacturing workers still growing, and open unemployment concentrated among youth. Labor scarcity, China's core driver, is absent. (3) GDP PER CAPITA — China's per-capita GDP was roughly US$7,000-8,000 when Made in China 2025 launched in 2015 and about US$13,000 today; Indonesia is roughly US$5,000-5,500 in 2025, i.e. at China's ~2011-2013 level, consistent with the 12-15 year lag estimate. (4) MANUFACTURING SCALE AND DENSITY — automation economics depend on volume per SKU and on a dense supplier ecosystem within a short radius. China's ~30% share of global MVA and its cluster geography (an entire electronics supply chain within 100 km of Shenzhen) is unreproducible; Indonesia's ~US$255 billion MVA is ~1.5% of global and is geographically fragmented across islands. (5) ELECTRICITY — a dark factory needs 24/7 stable power; PLN reliability and industrial tariffs outside Java-Bali remain a binding constraint. (6) TECHNICIAN BASE — China built a mass base of mechatronics, PLC, robot-programming and maintenance technicians via a thousand-plus vocational colleges plus the 智能制造工程 undergraduate major; Indonesia's SMK/politeknik output is misaligned, with employers reporting they cannot find staff who can operate and troubleshoot automation systems. (7) CAPITAL COST — Chinese firms accessed subsidized equipment-renewal loans and local-government robot purchase subsidies; Indonesian SMEs face double-digit commercial lending rates and no equivalent capex incentive beyond limited tax allowances. (8) DOMESTIC ROBOT SUPPLY — China localized reducers, servos and controllers before scaling; Indonesia imports 100% of robot hardware, exposing adoption to rupiah volatility and TKDN local-content rules that can perversely raise automation cost.
indikator_pemantauan: LEADING INDICATORS THAT THE TREND IS LANDING. (1) TRADE DATA — HS 8479.50 (industrial robots) and 8428/8427 (AGVs, handling equipment) import volumes and values into Indonesia, monitored quarterly via BPS; a sustained doubling is the cleanest early signal. (2) FDI FILINGS — BKPM/Kementerian Investasi announcements of greenfield plants with stated capacity-per-worker ratios; a plant announcing 150,000 units/year with under 2,000 workers (BYD Subang's profile) is an automation signal disguised as an investment headline. (3) JOB POSTINGS — counts on JobStreet/LinkedIn/Kalibrr for 'robot programmer', 'PLC engineer', 'automation engineer', 'MES engineer', 'maintenance mechatronics', 'vision system engineer'; a rising ratio of automation-engineer postings to production-operator postings within the same firms is the single most diagnostic indicator. (4) DISTRIBUTOR AND INTEGRATOR FOOTPRINT — new Indonesian offices or authorized distributors for Chinese robot brands (Unitree, JAKA, Dobot, Estun, Inovance, Siasun) and the client counts they publish; Halo Robotics' 900+ client base is the current baseline. (5) TRADEMARK AND COMPANY REGISTRATIONS — DJKI trademark filings and OSS/NIB registrations under KBLI codes for industrial machinery installation, robotics services and industrial automation engineering. (6) EDUCATION SUPPLY — new prodi approvals from Kemendikbudristek/Kemdiktisaintek for robotics, mechatronics, AI and smart manufacturing (UNIKOM's Teknik Robotika dan AI from 2025/2026, UNAIR's TRKB from July 2025, UI's S1 Kecerdasan Artifisial from 2026/2027, Politeknik AI Budi Mulia Dua); a sharp acceleration in approvals is a 3-4 year leading indicator of workforce readiness. (7) POLICY SIGNALS — Kemenperin INDI 4.0 assessment counts and average scores, any tax-allowance or super-deduction scheme specifically for automation capex, and any TKDN rule change affecting robot imports. (8) UTILITY DATA — industrial electricity consumption per unit of manufacturing output and per worker in key estates (Cikarang, Karawang, Batang, Subang); rising kWh-per-worker with flat headcount is a hard physical signature of automation. (9) LABOR-SIDE SIGNALS — union (KSPI/KSPSI) statements specifically naming automation rather than import competition as the cause of layoffs; the first such national dispute will mark the political arrival of the trend. (10) HUMANOID-SPECIFIC — customs entries of humanoid/quadruped robots, demonstrations at Indonesia Manufacturing/Manufacturing Indonesia expos, and any SOE (Pertamina, PLN, Antam, Krakatau Steel, Danantara portfolio) tender specifying robotic inspection.
hambatan_transfer: (1) WAGE ARBITRAGE STILL FAVORS HUMANS — at ~US$1.85/hour minimum wage, a robot cell costing US$50,000-120,000 installed has a payback of 5-8 years in most labor-intensive Indonesian sectors versus 2-3 years in China in 2013-2015; severance and social-security costs of dismissing workers further worsen the math. (2) POLITICAL ECONOMY OF JOBS — the Prabowo administration has explicitly directed economic ministers and the Dewan Ekonomi Nasional to strengthen LABOR-INTENSIVE (padat karya) industry and to bring it into the National Strategic Projects framework; automation cuts directly against the government's headline employment objective, so state incentives point the other way. (3) SME STRUCTURE AND CAPITAL COST — most Indonesian manufacturers are SMEs with short order books, high SKU variability and no access to cheap capex financing; automation requires volume stability they do not have. (4) SKILLS DEFICIT — employers consistently report an inability to find people who can operate, program and troubleshoot automation; vocational output is small and misaligned, and there is no national robot-technician certification of scale. (5) INFRASTRUCTURE — power reliability and industrial tariffs, plus archipelagic logistics that fragment production runs and prevent the cluster density automation rewards. (6) IMPORT DEPENDENCE AND FX RISK — 100% of robot hardware is imported; rupiah depreciation directly raises automation costs, and TKDN local-content requirements in public and some private procurement can penalize imported automation. (7) MAINTENANCE AND SPARES ECOSYSTEM — limited local service capability means downtime risk, which risk-averse plant managers price heavily. (8) DATA AND IT MATURITY — smart manufacturing requires MES/ERP integration and clean process data; many Indonesian plants still run on paper and spreadsheets, so the digital substrate for Industry 4.0 does not exist even where robots do. (9) LOW TRUST IN GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS — Making Indonesia 4.0's 25%-of-GDP-by-2030 target is visibly off-track (19% in 2024), which has eroded private-sector belief that the roadmap will be resourced.
faktor_pembatal_transfer: STRUCTURAL REASONS THE CHINESE FORM OF THIS TREND WILL NEVER FULLY ARRIVE. (1) THE DEMOGRAPHIC PREMISE IS INVERTED. China automated because it was running out of workers — the working-age population peaked in 2011-2013 and manufacturing employment fell 30+ million while output rose. Indonesia has a demographic bonus running to roughly 2035-2040, 20.3 million and still-growing manufacturing workers, and a political imperative to absorb 2-3 million labor-market entrants per year. A lights-out factory solves a problem Indonesia does not have and creates one it cannot afford. (2) SCALE AND CLUSTER DENSITY CANNOT BE REPLICATED. Xiaomi's dark factory is economic because it makes ~10 million identical handsets a year against a supply chain where every component is available within a day's drive. Indonesia's manufacturing value added is ~1.5% of the world's against China's ~30%; no Indonesian plant has the SKU volume or supplier density to amortize a fully automated line. (3) ARCHIPELAGIC GEOGRAPHY AND LOGISTICS COST. Automation's returns compound with just-in-time flow; Indonesia's inter-island shipping costs and lead-time variance force buffer inventory and batch production, which structurally reduces the payoff from flow automation. This is a permanent geographic feature, not a fixable policy gap. (4) NO DOMESTIC CAPITAL-GOODS INDUSTRY. China's automation was self-reinforcing because it built the robots it installed — creating jobs, engineers, and export revenue that funded further adoption. Indonesia importing robots means automation is a pure import-substitution-of-labor transaction with no domestic multiplier; every efficiency gain leaks abroad as equipment payments. Without a machine-tool and components base, Indonesia can be an automation CONSUMER but never an automation ECONOMY. (5) THE COMPARATIVE ADVANTAGE CONFLICT. Indonesia's pitch to relocating Chinese manufacturers is cheap labor plus resources plus market access. A firm that relocates to Indonesia and then fully automates has no reason to be in Indonesia rather than staying in a Chinese dark factory — so the relocation vector self-limits the automation vector. Chinese firms will bring SELECTIVE automation (quality-critical and hazardous steps) while keeping labor-intensive steps manual, producing a hybrid 'Industry 2.5-3.5' factory that is neither Chinese-style dark nor traditionally manual. (6) ELECTRICITY AND GRID ECONOMICS. Fully automated 24/7 production shifts the cost base from wages to power; with Indonesian industrial tariffs and reliability outside Java, the substitution is far less attractive than in Guangdong or Jiangsu. (7) POLICY DIRECTION. The state is actively subsidizing labor-intensity, not automation. NET PREDICTION: Indonesia will get automation ENCLAVES (foreign-owned, export-oriented, capital-intensive, in automotive/EV, batteries, electronics, and mineral processing) inside a much larger manual manufacturing economy — a dual-track structure, not the Chinese uniform transformation.
tahun_masuk_indonesia: Already arrived, in layers. Basic industrial robotics entered with Japanese automotive investment in the 1990s-2000s and deepened from roughly 2010-2015 (Toyota, Daihatsu, Denso). The Korean wave arrived with Hyundai's Cikarang plant (2021-2022). The CHINESE smart-manufacturing wave — which is the subject of this research — arrived in 2024-2026 with Wuling's stated I2MS conversion plan and BYD's Subang plant beginning operation in 2026, alongside the tariff-driven relocation of Chinese electronics, textile and component manufacturers (16 MoUs worth IDR 36.4 trillion signed November 2025; China third-largest FDI source at US$2.2 billion in Q1 2026). Embodied AI/humanoid robots entered at pilot scale in 2026, through Halo Robotics as Unitree's sole official distributor, in inspection and facility-documentation roles.
tahun_mainstream_indonesia: Roughly 2032-2036 for industrial robotics to become normal across mid-sized Indonesian manufacturers (not just foreign-owned auto/electronics plants). The gating variable is wages: Indonesian manufacturing labor cost needs to reach roughly US$3.50-4.50/hour in real terms to replicate China's 2013 automation trigger, which at current 6-9% nominal wage growth implies the early-to-mid 2030s — coinciding with the tail of the demographic bonus. Integrated smart factories (MES + IoT + analytics) become mainstream in large enterprises somewhat earlier, roughly 2029-2033, because their driver is quality/traceability for export compliance rather than labor cost. Humanoid robots in routine industrial use: not before 2035-2040 at scale, though visible pilot deployments will be common by 2028-2030. [uncertain — highly sensitive to wage trajectory, rupiah, and whether the government reverses its labor-intensive policy stance]
tahun_puncak_indonesia: Approximately 2040-2048 for the automation build-out to peak, i.e. the period of maximum annual robot installations and maximum labor-displacement pressure. This aligns with the end of Indonesia's demographic bonus (~2035-2040), when the workforce stops growing and labor costs rise structurally — the exact conjunction that triggered China's 2013 takeoff, arriving in Indonesia roughly 25 years later. Embodied AI/humanoid peak would follow in the late 2040s. Caveat: a peak in ADOPTION is not guaranteed to arrive at all if Indonesia's manufacturing sector continues to shrink as a share of GDP — in the pessimistic scenario, Indonesia deindustrializes past the point where large-scale automation ever becomes relevant, and the 'peak' never materializes. [uncertain — this is a 15-20 year extrapolation with wide error bands]
skenario_percepatan: (1) A sharp rise in Indonesian minimum wages or a labor-cost shock (e.g. large annual UMP increases plus stricter severance enforcement) that flips robot payback below three years. (2) Aggressive Chinese equipment price dumping driven by domestic overcapacity and involution, cutting robot cell costs by 40-60%. (3) Export-market compliance pressure — EU CBAM, traceability, and quality certification requirements that only digitized/automated plants can satisfy. (4) A large state-backed anchor project: Danantara or an SOE funding a flagship smart factory, or a national automation tax super-deduction. (5) Massive Chinese greenfield FDI in EV, battery and electronics with automation specifications written into the investment agreement. (6) A demographic surprise — faster-than-expected fertility decline compressing the labor surplus. (7) Cheap robot-as-a-service / leasing models that convert capex into opex for SMEs, which is how Chinese cobot vendors are already penetrating Southeast Asian SMEs.
dampak_lapangan_kerja: JOBS AT RISK (in the enclaves first, then diffusing): production operators on repetitive assembly, welding, painting, palletizing and packing lines; manual visual QC inspectors (already the first task humanoids and machine vision take, per the 2026 Indonesian pilots); material handlers and forklift operators (displaced by AGVs/AMRs); warehouse pickers; basic machine minders; line supervisors whose role is headcount management rather than process engineering; and — critically for Indonesia — the entry-level factory job that has historically been the ladder from rural underemployment into the formal economy and into BPJS coverage. Indonesia's textile and footwear sectors already lost roughly 250,000 jobs across 60 factory closures in 2022-2024 and 42,000-70,000 more in H1 2025, and labor absorption in labor-intensive sectors collapsed from 471,972 (2024) to 202,244 in H1 2026 alone — but that destruction is currently driven by import competition, weak demand and cost pressure, NOT robots. The danger is sequencing: automation will land on a labor market already scarred, so its marginal jobs will be far more painful than China's were, because China automated into a tight labor market that reabsorbed displaced workers into services and logistics, while Indonesia would automate into a slack one. JOBS THAT CHANGE: maintenance technicians shift from mechanical repair to mechatronics and predictive diagnostics; QC shifts from inspecting to validating vision-system outputs and managing false positives; production planners shift to MES/data work; procurement shifts toward spares and service contracts. JOBS CREATED (far fewer than lost, and requiring different people): robot programmers and integrators, PLC/SCADA engineers, machine-vision and MES engineers, industrial data analysts, robot maintenance and calibration technicians, industrial cybersecurity specialists, systems-integration project managers, and automation sales/service roles at distributors. The Chinese precedent is unambiguous on the arithmetic: manufacturing employment fell from ~115 million (2013) to under 85 million (2025) — a 26% decline — while output and exports hit records; MOHRSS's response of recognizing 72 new occupations, 20+ AI-related, each seeding 300,000-500,000 jobs, does not come close to offsetting 30 million losses. For Indonesia the specific risk is that the country's manufacturing employment plateau (~20.3 million) becomes a permanent ceiling reached at roughly 19% of GDP, meaning Indonesia never gets the mass formal-employment phase that industrialization historically delivered. [uncertain — Indonesian automation-attributable job losses are not separately measured and are currently confounded with trade-driven closures]
dampak_kelas_menengah: Ambiguous and polarizing. THE PATHWAY THAT CLOSES: for the lower-middle class, a formal factory job with BPJS Kesehatan and Ketenagakerjaan coverage, a UMP-anchored wage and a payslip that qualifies for a KPR mortgage or motorcycle credit has been the principal escalator into middle-class status — and it is exactly this rung that automation removes first. Indonesia's middle class has already been contracting (the 'aspiring middle class' has grown while the middle class proper has shrunk since 2019), and automation removes the most reliable remaining ladder. THE PATHWAY THAT OPENS: a small technical middle class of automation engineers, integrators and mechatronics technicians whose wages rise sharply because supply is scarce — Indonesian employers already report they cannot find people who can troubleshoot automation systems. Expect a widening wage gap WITHIN factories: a robot maintenance technician may earn 3-5x a line operator, versus 1.5-2x today. CONSUMPTION EFFECT: falling factory employment weakens the wage-driven consumption base that Indonesian retail, property and motorcycle finance depend on, which is already visible in the 2025-2026 demand weakness. NET: automation in Indonesia is likely to be middle-class-hollowing rather than middle-class-creating unless the technician pipeline is built at scale first — the opposite of China, where two decades of manufacturing surplus had already created a large middle class BEFORE robots arrived, giving the country a cushion Indonesia does not have.
dampak_daerah_non_jawa: Highly uneven, and mostly Java-concentrated in the near term. JAVA: automation is and will remain concentrated in the industrial corridor — Bekasi/Cikarang, Karawang, Purwakarta, Subang (BYD/Subang Smartpolitan), Batang (KIT), Gresik/Sidoarjo, and Sememi — because that is where automotive, electronics and appliance plants, reliable power, ports and the technician base are. Java is also where the displacement will be felt, since it holds the bulk of the 20.3 million manufacturing workers. BATAM/BINTAN: the second concentration, driven by electronics EMS and tariff-driven Chinese relocation; Batam is the most likely site of Indonesia's first genuinely high-automation electronics plant. NON-JAVA RESOURCE CORRIDORS: a distinct and under-appreciated vector — automation is arriving fastest in mining and mineral processing (Morowali and Weda Bay nickel/battery complexes, coal, oil & gas), where robotic inspection, autonomous haulage, drones and gas-sensing quadrupeds are already being adopted for SAFETY and HAZARD reasons rather than labor cost. This means Kalimantan, Sulawesi and Maluku may see embodied-AI robots in industrial use BEFORE most Javanese factories do, but in inspection and hazardous-environment roles rather than assembly. THE REST OF THE ARCHIPELAGO: NTT, NTB, Papua, and most of Sumatra outside Batam/Medan have negligible manufacturing exposure and will experience this trend indirectly — through fewer job openings in Java for migrant workers, and through remittance decline. RISK: automation therefore widens the Java/non-Java gap in HIGH-SKILL employment (automation engineers cluster in Java and Batam) while the non-Java resource regions get robots without getting the engineering jobs that come with them, since those are staffed by expatriates or Java-based contractors.
jurusan_terancam: PROGRAMS WHOSE GRADUATE VALUE ERODES IF THEY DO NOT CHANGE CONTENT: (1) SMK vocational streams narrowly built around single-machine manual operation — Teknik Pemesinan (conventional lathe/milling only), Teknik Pengelasan (manual welding without robot-welding or WPS/inspection content), Teknik Sepeda Motor/Kendaraan Ringan taught on ICE-only platforms, Tata Busana/Garmen for basic sewing operations, and Teknik Elektronika Industri taught without PLC/HMI/industrial networking. (2) D3 Teknik Mesin and D3 Teknik Industri programs whose curriculum stops at conventional machining, time-and-motion study and manual quality control — the tasks most directly absorbed by CNC, robotic cells and machine vision. (3) S1 Teknik Industri where the core skill taught is manual line balancing and work measurement rather than simulation, digital twin, MES and supply-chain analytics. (4) Manajemen Operasi / Manajemen Produksi tracks in business schools that teach production planning without any data or systems layer. (5) Purely mechanical S1 Teknik Mesin with no mechatronics, control, or embedded-systems content — the archetype of a degree that was safe for 40 years and is now the wrong half of the discipline. IMPORTANT CAVEAT specific to Indonesia: the threat to these programs over the next 5-8 years comes far more from DEINDUSTRIALIZATION and factory closures than from robots — a welding graduate in 2026 is more likely to be unemployed because the plant shut than because a robot took the seam. The automation threat becomes dominant in the 2030s. Note also that Indonesia's 2025-2026 nomenclature change (Teknik → Rekayasa) is a renaming, not a content reform, and does nothing to address this.
jurusan_dibutuhkan: HIGHEST-VALUE SKILLS AND PROGRAMS: (1) MECHATRONICS AND ROBOTICS ENGINEERING — the single scarcest profile in Indonesian industry: robot programming (KUKA KRL, ABB RAPID, Fanuc TP, plus increasingly Chinese controller stacks from Estun/Inovance/JAKA), robot cell design, end-effector and fixture design, safety standards (ISO 10218, ISO/TS 15066 for collaborative robots). (2) INDUSTRIAL AUTOMATION AND CONTROL — PLC (Siemens TIA, Mitsubishi, Omron, and Chinese Inovance), SCADA/HMI, industrial networking (Profinet, EtherCAT, OPC-UA), instrumentation and process control; this is the highest employability-per-year-of-study skill in Indonesian manufacturing right now. (3) MACHINE VISION AND APPLIED AI FOR MANUFACTURING — defect detection, OCR/traceability, edge inference deployment; distinct from generic data science because it requires optics, lighting and process knowledge. (4) MES / INDUSTRIAL IT AND OT-IT INTEGRATION — MES/ERP integration, industrial data engineering, digital twin and simulation (Plant Simulation, FlexSim, AnyLogic); the layer Indonesia is weakest in because most plants have no digital substrate. (5) MAINTENANCE ENGINEERING AND RELIABILITY — predictive maintenance, vibration and thermographic analysis, spares management; automation does not remove maintenance, it upgrades it, and this is the most accessible upskilling path for existing technicians. (6) INDUSTRIAL CYBERSECURITY (OT security, IEC 62443) — near-zero domestic supply, rising demand as plants connect. (7) EMBODIED AI / ROBOT LEARNING — ROS/ROS2, reinforcement and imitation learning, sim-to-real, VLA (vision-language-action) models; the frontier layer where China is now creating a formal undergraduate discipline. (8) HYBRID PROFILES that Indonesia specifically needs — automation SALES ENGINEERS and SYSTEM INTEGRATORS who can scope, cost and justify an automation project to a skeptical SME owner; this commercial-technical hybrid is the actual bottleneck in Indonesian diffusion, more than pure engineering talent. (9) ENERGY AND POWER ENGINEERING for industrial reliability, since automation shifts the constraint from labor to power quality.
china_education_response: China restructured higher education around this trend with unusual speed and force, in three stages. STAGE 1 — SMART MANUFACTURING MAJOR (2017-2020): the Ministry of Education approved 智能制造工程 (Intelligent Manufacturing Engineering) as a new undergraduate major in 2017-2018; within about five years it had been established at 300+ institutions, becoming one of the fastest-spreading new majors in Chinese history, alongside 机器人工程 (Robotics Engineering), which had already been approved in 2015-2016 and spread to 300+ universities. Vocational colleges added industrial robot operation and maintenance (工业机器人技术) programs at scale, tied directly to the Robot+ application plan. STAGE 2 — MASSIVE PRUNING (14th Five-Year Plan, 2021-2025): China added 10,200 new undergraduate program points nationally while cancelling or suspending enrollment in 12,200 — a net REDUCTION, with cumulative adjustment exceeding 30% of all programs and the annual adjustment ratio passing 10% for the first time in 2026. Programs eliminated in bulk included public administration, information management, marketing, clothing/apparel design, product design, and many low-differentiation business and management degrees. This is the decisive contrast with Indonesia: China did not merely ADD new majors, it FORCIBLY CLOSED obsolete ones at national scale. STAGE 3 — EMBODIED AI AS A DISCIPLINE (2026): on 28 April 2026 the MOE released the 2026 Undergraduate Program Catalogue adding 38 new majors, including — for the first time — 具身智能 (Embodied Intelligence), 脑机科学与技术 (Brain-Computer Science and Technology), 未来机器人 (Future Robotics), 农业机器人 (Agricultural Robotics), 生物制造 (Biomanufacturing), and 交叉工程 (Interdisciplinary Engineering), with 11 existing and 4 brand-new programs placed under a newly created INTERDISCIPLINARY (交叉学科) degree category. Nine universities — including Harbin Institute of Technology and Beihang (BUAA) — were authorized to open the Embodied Intelligence major with gaokao admissions starting the same year. The full pipeline was closed in the same period: MIIT established a Humanoid Robots and Embodied AI Standardization Technical Committee in December 2025 and published the first Humanoid Robotics and Embodied Intelligence Standard System in February 2026, while MOHRSS recognized 72 new occupations in five years (20+ AI-related), giving graduates formal occupational categories, certification pathways and wage scales to enter. LESSON: China aligned MAJOR + STANDARD + OCCUPATION CODE + STATE PROCUREMENT simultaneously, so that a new degree had a defined job at the other end. Indonesia currently does the first step only.
respons_kebijakan_china: POLICIES ADOPTED WHILE PROMOTING THE TREND: Made in China 2025 (May 2015) with localization targets for robots and core components; the Robot Industry Development Plan 2016-2020; the Robot+ Application Action Plan (January 2023) mandating robot deployment across ten sectors; the six-ministry Smart Factory Gradient Cultivation Action (2025) creating a four-tier certification ladder (basic/advanced/excellence/leading) that channels subsidies and prestige; MIIT's Humanoid Robot Innovation Guidance (November 2023) setting 2025 mass-production and 2027 world-leading targets; the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) elevating embodied AI to a national 'future industry'; and the MIIT+SASAC joint real-world training campaign (2026) ordering deployment of 10,000 humanoids across 100+ scenarios — using state-owned enterprises as guaranteed first customers to bridge the commercialization valley of death. POLICIES ADOPTED AFTER PROBLEMS EMERGED — the part Indonesia should study: (1) LABOR-SIDE CORRECTION — MOHRSS announced on 27 January 2026 that China would issue a dedicated policy document on responding to AI's employment impact, having previously treated automation purely as an industrial-upgrading win; it also created 72 new official occupations in five years to give displaced and new workers formal categories and certification routes. (2) ANTI-INVOLUTION ENFORCEMENT — after the EV price war destroyed sector profitability, Beijing began explicitly campaigning against 内卷式竞争 (involutionary competition) in 2025-2026, and the humanoid sector is now being watched for the same pathology, with 140+ companies and 330+ products already in the market. (3) STANDARDIZATION BEFORE SATURATION — establishing the humanoid/embodied-AI standards committee and standard system BEFORE mass deployment, to avoid the safety and interoperability chaos that followed the e-bike and EV battery booms. (4) SOCIAL SECURITY PORTABILITY — reforms to hukou and social insurance portability were partly a response to displaced manufacturing workers needing to move into service and gig work. WHAT INDONESIA SHOULD ADOPT PREEMPTIVELY: (a) require large automation-related investments to file a workforce transition plan (retraining or redeployment commitments) as a condition of tax incentives — before automation is widespread, when the requirement is cheap to impose; (b) create the occupational standards and certification (SKKNI) for automation technician roles NOW, so the training market has a target; (c) tie any automation capex incentive to a matched training spend, the mechanism Singapore used successfully; (d) build automation-displacement into BPJS Ketenagakerjaan's JKP (unemployment benefit) design and funding assumptions, which currently assume cyclical not structural displacement; (e) avoid China's mistake of measuring success purely by installation counts — measure productivity per worker and wage growth, not robots deployed.
rekomendasi_kebijakan_indonesia: (1) SEQUENCE CORRECTLY — Indonesia's binding problem in 2026 is deindustrialization and weak manufacturing competitiveness, not robots. Policy should target automation as a COMPETITIVENESS tool for the plants that must survive globally (automotive, electronics, batteries, food processing for export) while explicitly NOT subsidizing automation in labor-intensive sectors where Indonesia still holds cost advantage. A blanket automation subsidy would destroy jobs the country cannot replace. (2) BUILD THE TECHNICIAN PIPELINE FIRST — the highest-return intervention is a national automation-technician program: SKKNI competency standards plus certification for robot programming, PLC/SCADA, machine vision and predictive maintenance; convert 100-200 SMK and politeknik programs to automation-capable with real equipment (not simulators), and require Chinese/Japanese/Korean investors receiving tax holidays to co-fund and staff training centers, as a condition of the incentive. Kemenperin's 5,472 vocational graduates in 2025 must become a five-digit-per-year figure. (3) MANDATE TRANSITION PLANS — require any investment above a threshold that reduces headcount-per-unit-output to file a workforce transition plan with Kemnaker as a condition of fiscal facilities; make it administrative, not punitive. (4) FIX THE CAPITAL COST FOR SMEs, NOT THE ROBOT PRICE — support robot-as-a-service, leasing and shared automation service centers at industrial estates so SMEs can access automation without capex; this diffuses productivity without concentrating ownership. (5) DO NOT LET TKDN BLOCK AUTOMATION WHILE ALSO NOT CONCEDING THE CAPITAL-GOODS SECTOR — negotiate technology-transfer and local-content commitments in robot assembly, end-effectors, fixtures, cabling and systems integration (the achievable 40% of the value chain) rather than attempting to localize reducers and servos, which China took 15 years and state capital to achieve. (6) INSTRUMENT THE PHENOMENON — BPS and Kemenperin should publish an annual robot installation and density series (partnering with IFR) plus an automation module in the manufacturing survey; Indonesia currently cannot manage this trend because it cannot measure it. (7) PREEMPTIVE SOCIAL PROTECTION — stress-test BPJS Ketenagakerjaan's JKP against structural rather than cyclical displacement, and extend coverage design toward workers who will move from formal factory work into informal gig work. (8) LEVERAGE THE FDI MOMENT — with China as the third-largest FDI source and tariff-driven relocation underway, Indonesia has unusual bargaining power right now; use it to require engineering job localization (a minimum share of automation engineers hired locally and trained), not just assembly jobs. (9) ELECTRICITY RELIABILITY as industrial policy — automation is unbankable without stable power; grid quality in industrial estates is an automation policy, not just an energy policy. (10) LEARN CHINA'S ANTI-INVOLUTION LESSON EARLY — do not create a subsidy race between provinces/estates for robot installation counts, which in China produced volume without profitability.
peluang_bisnis: (1) SYSTEMS INTEGRATION AND AUTOMATION ENGINEERING SERVICES — the largest and most defensible opportunity. Chinese and Japanese robot vendors need local partners to scope, install, program, commission and maintain; system integration is 56% of China's own robot industry value (RMB 139.5 billion of RMB 247.5 billion in 2025), and in Indonesia it is almost entirely unserved by domestic firms. This is a services business requiring engineering talent, not capital. (2) ROBOT-AS-A-SERVICE / LEASING FOR SMEs — converting a US$60,000 capex decision into a monthly fee unlocks the mid-market that will otherwise never automate; combine with performance guarantees (paid per unit produced or per defect avoided). (3) MAINTENANCE, SPARES AND UPTIME CONTRACTS — the highest-margin, most recurring, least import-dependent segment; Indonesia's automation adoption is currently constrained by downtime fear, so whoever solves service solves adoption. (4) TRAINING AND CERTIFICATION — corporate academies, bootcamps and vocational partnerships for PLC, robot programming, machine vision and industrial IoT; demand is already documented (employers cannot find automation-capable staff) and the supply is essentially nil. (5) RETROFIT / LOW-COST AUTOMATION FOR IKM — cobots, pick-and-place cells, vision QC kits and simple AGVs priced for Indonesian SMEs in food processing, packaging, furniture and components; Chinese cobot pricing makes this newly viable. (6) DISTRIBUTION OF CHINESE ROBOTICS BRANDS — the Halo Robotics/Unitree model, extended to industrial arm and AMR brands (JAKA, Dobot, Estun, Inovance, Siasun) that need Indonesian channel partners as they push exports amid domestic overcapacity. (7) INSPECTION-ROBOTICS SERVICES FOR RESOURCES — quadruped and drone-based inspection, gas sensing and thermography sold as a SERVICE to mining, smelting, oil & gas and power plants in Kalimantan, Sulawesi and Sumatra, where safety and insurance economics justify it long before labor cost does; this is the fastest-monetizing embodied-AI niche in Indonesia today. (8) MES / INDUSTRIAL SOFTWARE LOCALIZED FOR INDONESIAN SMEs — lightweight production tracking, OEE and traceability software priced far below SAP/Siemens; most Indonesian plants need digitization before robotization, and this is a software business Indonesians can own outright. (9) END-EFFECTORS, FIXTURES, JIGS AND CABLING — the localizable 30-40% of an automation cell, achievable with existing Indonesian metalworking capability. (10) INDUSTRIAL ESTATE SERVICES — shared automation centers, power quality solutions and technician housing/training at Subang Smartpolitan, KIT Batang, Batam and Karawang, riding the Chinese relocation wave. (11) OT CYBERSECURITY consulting, an unserved category with regulatory tailwinds.
rekomendasi_individu_mahasiswa: PRIORITY SKILL STACK, in order of Indonesian employability per unit of effort: (1) PLC/SCADA competence (Siemens TIA Portal, Mitsubishi, Omron — add Inovance given the Chinese equipment wave) — this alone is currently the fastest route from a mechanical or electrical degree to a well-paid manufacturing job in Indonesia. (2) Robot programming on at least one platform plus safety standards (ISO 10218 / ISO-TS 15066); vendor certifications matter more than GPA to employers. (3) Python plus machine vision (OpenCV, then a deployment framework) — defect detection is the first automation task most Indonesian plants adopt. (4) ROS2 and simulation (Gazebo/Isaac) for anyone aiming at the embodied-AI frontier. (5) Electrical/mechanical fundamentals that do NOT go obsolete — control theory, pneumatics/hydraulics, tolerancing, GD&T. (6) Data literacy for operations: SQL, time-series analysis, OEE and statistical process control. (7) MANDARIN, seriously — the equipment, the manuals, the vendors, the plant managers and the investors on the Chinese relocation wave are increasingly Chinese; a mechatronics engineer who reads Chinese technical documentation is a scarce and highly paid asset in Indonesia, and this is a genuine arbitrage most Indonesian students ignore. (8) COMMERCIAL SKILL — the ability to build an ROI case and sell an automation project to an SME owner; Indonesia's bottleneck is as much commercial as technical, and technical-commercial hybrids will command premiums. STRATEGIC ADVICE: do not chase the humanoid hype for a career in Indonesia in the next 5-8 years — the jobs are in boring, unglamorous automation (PLC, maintenance, integration, MES), and that is precisely where the scarcity premium sits. Also strongly consider MAINTENANCE over pure design: automation multiplies maintenance demand and it cannot be offshored. For students in labor-intensive-sector-adjacent programs, prioritize mobility into automation-capable roles now, because the plant closures already underway will not wait for the robots.
rekomendasi_perguruan_tinggi: OPEN OR STRENGTHEN: (1) A proper Smart Manufacturing / Rekayasa Manufaktur Cerdas program modeled on China's 智能制造工程 (which reached 300+ Chinese universities within five years) — combining mechatronics, control, industrial IT and data, not just renaming Teknik Mesin. (2) D3/D4 Automation Technician programs with REAL equipment — a politeknik teaching robotics on simulators produces unemployable graduates; equipment partnerships with Fanuc/ABB/Mitsubishi and now Chinese vendors (Estun, Inovance, JAKA, Unitree) should be a condition of program approval. (3) Applied AI for Manufacturing tracks (machine vision, predictive maintenance) inside existing informatics faculties, which are currently teaching generic data science with no industrial context. (4) OT/Industrial Cybersecurity as a specialization. (5) An Embodied AI/Robot Learning research track at 3-5 leading institutions only (ITB, ITS, UI, UGM, PENS) — Indonesia should not spread this thinly across 100 campuses. RESTRUCTURE OR MERGE: conventional D3 Teknik Mesin and Teknik Industri programs whose curricula end at manual machining and time-and-motion study; Teknik Elektronika Industri without PLC and industrial networking; and the large number of low-differentiation management/business programs — China cancelled or suspended 12,200 undergraduate program points in five years while adding 10,200, a NET reduction; Indonesia adds programs but almost never closes them, which is why the automation-relevant share of graduates barely moves. INSTITUTIONAL REFORMS: (a) make dual-system industry placement (minimum 6-12 months in a real automated plant) mandatory, following the German/Chinese vocational model; (b) certify LECTURERS on industrial equipment, not just students — Indonesia's constraint is faculty who have never programmed a robot; (c) build shared regional automation labs at industrial estates (Cikarang, Karawang, Batam, Batang, Surabaya) that multiple campuses and local SMEs use, rather than every campus buying one underused robot arm; (d) require every new automation program to be launched WITH a defined SKKNI occupational standard and industry hiring commitment, replicating China's major+standard+occupation-code alignment; (e) reverse the sequencing error — Indonesia is opening AI and robotics degrees (UNIKOM 2025/2026, UNAIR TRKB July 2025, UI S1 Kecerdasan Artifisial 2026/2027, Politeknik AI Budi Mulia Dua) faster than it is producing automation TECHNICIANS, when the industrial demand is roughly ten technicians per engineer.
dampak_negatif_china: (1) THE LARGEST PEACETIME MANUFACTURING JOB LOSS IN HISTORY — manufacturing employment fell from roughly 115 million in 2013 to under 85 million in 2025, over 30 million jobs lost, while output and exports set records; this decoupling of output from employment is the trend's defining social cost. (2) UNEQUAL INCIDENCE ON THE VULNERABLE — empirical research finds a one-standard-deviation increase in robot exposure reduces employment probability by about 5 percentage points, raises labor-force exit by about 1 point and self-reported unemployment by about 4 points, with effects concentrated among low-skilled, male, prime-age and older workers — precisely the group with the least retraining capacity and, for migrant workers, the least social protection. (3) AUTOMATION EXPOSURE NOW PREDICTS LIFE OUTCOMES BETTER THAN FAMILY BACKGROUND — research on social mobility finds a worker's automation susceptibility has become a more powerful predictor of economic trajectory than parental status, meaning technology has become a new axis of inequality layered on top of the hukou divide. (4) DISPLACED WORKERS FELL INTO GIG WORK, NOT BETTER JOBS — a large share of ex-factory workers moved into food delivery, ride-hailing and logistics, trading stable (if hard) formal employment for platform work with worse protection and lower ceilings; China now has roughly 200 million flexible workers. (5) INVOLUTION AND PROFITLESS GROWTH — the robotics sector itself replicated the EV pathology: 140+ humanoid companies, 330+ products, 60+ humanoid OEMs, brutal price wars and collapsing margins, with Caixin reporting in June 2026 that founders and investors fear a repeat of the EV race to the bottom; volume records coexist with sector-wide unprofitability. (6) CAPITAL MISALLOCATION AND ZOMBIE CAPACITY — provincial subsidy competition produced duplicative robot plants and 'smart factory' showcases built for certification rather than economics; overcapacity is now an acknowledged national problem. (7) REGIONAL DEVASTATION IN OLD MANUFACTURING BELTS — automation compounded the northeast's (Dongbei) decline and hollowed out inland cities that never got the automation industry, only lost the assembly work. (8) DEFERRED POLICY RESPONSE — Beijing treated automation purely as industrial upgrading for a decade and only in January 2026 announced it would issue a dedicated document on AI's employment impact, meaning a decade of displacement occurred without a labor-transition framework.
risiko_sosial_indonesia: (1) AUTOMATION LANDING ON AN ALREADY-WOUNDED LABOR MARKET — unlike China, which automated into labor scarcity, Indonesia would automate into slack: 250,000 textile jobs already lost across 60 closures (2022-2024), 42,000-70,000 layoffs in H1 2025, PMI at 46.7 in April 2025, and labor absorption in labor-intensive sectors collapsing from 471,972 (2024) to 202,244 in H1 2026. Robots arriving into this would be a second shock on top of an unhealed first one, with no reabsorption capacity. (2) PREMATURE CLOSURE OF THE INDUSTRIALIZATION LADDER — Indonesia may never get the mass formal-manufacturing-employment phase that lifted Korea, China and Vietnam; manufacturing could peak permanently near 19% of GDP and ~20 million workers, leaving the demographic bonus (running to ~2035-2040) unabsorbed. This is the single largest social risk in this entire domain. (3) ENCLAVE ECONOMY AND FOREIGN-OWNED PRODUCTIVITY — automation concentrated in foreign-owned plants means productivity gains accrue to foreign capital and imported equipment vendors while employment costs are borne locally; Indonesia gets the displacement without the automation industry. (4) YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT AMPLIFICATION — Indonesian youth unemployment is already among the highest in ASEAN; entry-level operator roles are the first automated, removing the first rung for exactly the cohort most at risk. (5) INFORMALIZATION AND GIG ABSORPTION — displaced workers will flow into ojol, warung and informal trade, replicating China's gig absorption but WITHOUT China's density economics or platform earnings levels, and with weaker social protection; BPJS coverage would fall as formal jobs shrink. (6) WIDENING JAVA/NON-JAVA AND SKILL DIVIDES — automation engineering jobs cluster in Java and Batam while resource regions get inspection robots operated by outsiders. (7) REGULATORY VACUUM — Indonesia has no automation displacement framework, no robot-safety standard enforcement regime, no occupational standards for automation roles, and no measurement of robot installation; the trend could be well advanced before the state can see it. (8) POLITICAL BACKLASH RISK — a highly visible Chinese-owned automated plant employing few Indonesians is combustible material in an environment already sensitive to Chinese investment and foreign worker (TKA) issues; the first mass layoff publicly blamed on robots at a Chinese-owned facility would be a significant political event. (9) SAFETY AND STANDARDS GAP — imported robots deployed without ISO 10218/TS 15066 enforcement, by undertrained integrators, in plants with weak safety culture, is a foreseeable industrial-accident pathway.
unintended_consequences: (1) IN CHINA — automation intended to preserve manufacturing competitiveness ALSO destroyed the domestic consumption base that manufacturing wages funded, contributing to the demand weakness and deflationary pressure now afflicting the economy; robots solved the supply problem and worsened the demand problem. (2) Automation success made China SO cost-competitive that it triggered the tariff and de-risking wave that is now pushing its own manufacturers offshore — the very phenomenon transmitting this trend to Indonesia. (3) The robot industry became a new involution arena, so the sector built to escape low-margin competition reproduced low-margin competition one layer up. (4) Dark factories reduced not just labor but LIGHTING, HVAC and canteen/dormitory infrastructure — quietly eliminating an entire ecosystem of ancillary jobs (cleaners, cooks, security, dormitory staff, local food vendors) that never appears in manufacturing employment statistics; the true employment footprint of a factory is much larger than its payroll, and this is systematically underestimated in displacement analysis. (5) PREDICTED FOR INDONESIA — automation may arrive not as a wave of robots but as an ABSENCE: new plants that simply never hire at the ratios their predecessors did, so there is no layoff event to protest, no headline, and no policy trigger. Jobs that are never created are politically invisible, which is why this trend will likely be under-governed in Indonesia. (6) TKDN local-content rules designed to build domestic industry may perversely SLOW automation in ways that reduce competitiveness without creating a domestic robot industry, since Indonesia lacks the components base to benefit. (7) The Chinese relocation wave may deliver the WORST of both worlds: enough automation to limit job creation, but not enough to make Indonesian plants globally competitive, leaving a mid-technology trap. (8) Inspection robots entering via mining and oil & gas — for safety reasons — may normalize embodied AI in Indonesian industry through the back door, ahead of any assembly-line deployment and entirely outside the manufacturing policy conversation. (9) Cheap Chinese robots could paradoxically REVIVE some Indonesian manufacturing competitiveness against Vietnam and Bangladesh in mid-value segments, meaning selective automation might SAVE net jobs in specific export sectors even while cutting them per unit of output.
kelompok_rentan: (1) FACTORY OPERATORS WITH SMK-LEVEL EDUCATION AGED 35-50 — too senior to be cheap, too specialized in a single manual task to redeploy, too old for employers' informal hiring age limits; China's evidence shows displacement effects concentrate on prime-age and older low-skilled workers. (2) WOMEN IN LABOR-INTENSIVE MANUFACTURING — textiles, garments, footwear, electronics assembly and food processing are female-majority workforces and are the most automatable AND most import-exposed; the 250,000 textile job losses of 2022-2024 fell disproportionately on women, and automation would compound this. (3) FRESH SMK AND D3 GRADUATES in conventional machining, welding and general electronics whose training targets tasks now being automated and whose entry-level rung is disappearing first. (4) MIGRANT WORKERS FROM CENTRAL AND EAST JAVA in the Jabodetabek/Karawang industrial belt, whose remittances support rural households — displacement propagates outward to villages with no local formal alternative. (5) INFORMAL WORKERS IN THE FACTORY ECOSYSTEM — warung owners, kos-kosan landlords, ojek drivers, canteen and laundry workers around industrial estates, whose livelihoods depend on worker headcount and who are entirely invisible in employment statistics. (6) SME MANUFACTURERS (IKM) themselves — unable to afford automation, they lose orders to automated competitors and to imports, a business-owner class sliding out of the middle class. (7) YOUNG LABOR-MARKET ENTRANTS in non-Java regions who have no manufacturing employment pathway at all and for whom the ladder is closing before they reach it. (8) OLDER MAINTENANCE STAFF with purely mechanical skills who cannot make the mechatronics transition without structured retraining that currently does not exist at scale.
kasus_china: CASE 1 — XIAOMI CHANGPING DARK FACTORY: an 81,000 m² fully automated smartphone plant costing roughly RMB 2.4 billion (~US$330 million), running 24/7 with no humans on the production floor, no lighting and minimal HVAC, producing approximately one smartphone per second (~10 million units/year), orchestrated by Xiaomi's in-house HyperIMP platform where machines self-schedule and self-optimize. It is the canonical image of the trend and the one Indonesian policymakers and media have actually seen. CASE 2 — FOXCONN KUNSHAN: over 60,000 workers replaced by robots at a single plant, the clearest single-site displacement figure in the world and the event that made 'robots replacing Chinese factory workers' a global story. CASE 3 — THE 30-MILLION-JOB DECOUPLING: Chinese manufacturing employment fell from ~115 million (2013) to under 85 million (2025) while output rose to ~30% of global manufacturing value added and exports hit records — the definitive macro proof that manufacturing growth no longer implies manufacturing employment. CASE 4 — THE ROBOT INDUSTRY BECOMING AN EXPORT INDUSTRY: China produced 556,400 industrial robots in 2024 and over 770,000 in 2025 (+28%), with exports up 48.7% in 2025 and exceeding imports for the first time; domestic brands crossed 52.45% of the home market in 2024. The country that automated its factories now sells automation to everyone else — including, imminently, Indonesia. CASE 5 — UBTECH WALKER S IN AUTO PLANTS: humanoid robots deployed in real production at BYD, Foxconn, Zeekr and Audi-FAW facilities from 2024-2025, moving embodied AI from demo video to payroll substitute. CASE 6 — AGIBOT'S 10,000TH ROBOT: AgiBot scaled from 1,000 units (2025) to 5,000 to 10,000 within three months, rolling out its 10,000th general-purpose embodied robot (Expedition A3) in late March 2026 — the fastest ramp in humanoid history. CASE 7 — THE STATE AS FIRST CUSTOMER: MIIT and SASAC's 2026 joint action ordering commercial deployment of 10,000 humanoids across 100+ scenarios, using SOEs to guarantee demand — the mechanism that distinguishes Chinese industrial policy from Western subsidy. CASE 8 — THE WARNING CASE: 140+ humanoid companies, 330+ products, 60+ OEMs and collapsing prices in semi-humanoid segments, with Caixin (June 2026) reporting industry fears of an EV-style involutionary price war — the trend eating itself.
padanan_indonesia: (1) BYD SUBANG (Subang Smartpolitan, West Java) — US$1 billion, 108+ hectares, 150,000 units/year capacity, construction completed end-2025 and operational in 2026 producing the M6 and Atto 1. This is Indonesia's closest analogue to a modern Chinese automated plant, and the single most important object to watch: its robot-to-worker ratio will effectively set the benchmark for what Chinese-standard manufacturing in Indonesia looks like. (2) WULING/SGMW CIKARANG I2MS CONVERSION — SGMW Vice President Han Dehong stated the Indonesian plant will be progressively converted to the I2MS architecture used in Liuzhou, where autonomous mobile robots replace fixed conveyor rails. This is the first explicit commitment to import a Chinese smart-factory ARCHITECTURE (not just machines) into Indonesia. (3) HYUNDAI CIKARANG (HMMI) — Hyundai-built robots across stamping, welding and QC; the current Indonesian benchmark for robotized automotive assembly, and evidence that the Korean/Japanese channel, not the Chinese one, built Indonesia's existing robot base. (4) HALO ROBOTICS × UNITREE — Jakarta-based sole official Unitree distributor and service center with 900+ corporate and government clients, reporting in 2026 that humanoids are entering Indonesian manufacturing trials for repetitive visual inspection and facility documentation, and quadrupeds with gas sensors and cameras are doing routine inspection in mining, oil & gas and manufacturing. This is Indonesia's actual embodied-AI beachhead — inspection first, assembly later. (5) MAKING INDONESIA 4.0 + INDI 4.0 — the policy analogue to Made in China 2025, launched 4 April 2018, with a 25%-of-GDP-manufacturing-by-2030 target against an actual 18.98% in 2024; the gap between the two is the clearest available measure of Indonesia's execution deficit. (6) THE COUNTER-CASE — SRITEX, once Southeast Asia's largest integrated textile mill, ceased operations on 1 March 2025 laying off 10,660+ workers; alongside 60 textile factory closures affecting ~250,000 workers (2022-2024), it is a reminder that Indonesia's manufacturing crisis today is about survival, not automation, and that the automation debate is arriving on top of an industrial emergency.

catatan_kontradiksi_data: (1) CHINA ROBOT DENSITY — the most significant contradiction found. IFR World Robotics 2025 reports China at 166 robots per 10,000 manufacturing employees (2024), ranking ~22nd globally, while multiple secondary sources and earlier IFR reports cite 392 (2022) and 470 (2023), and some 2026 commentary claims 'over 400 per 10,000 in 2025'. The discrepancy is NOT a data error but a denominator restatement: IFR explicitly notes the 2025 figure uses updated labor-market data from China's National Bureau of Statistics, which revised manufacturing employment sharply upward. Analysts using pre-revision figures overstate China's density by roughly 3x. This research uses the 166 figure as current-official while noting that China's absolute stock (~2 million units, 54% of global installations) is undisputed and is the more meaningful measure. (2) INDONESIA AUTOMATION MARKET SIZE — PS Market Research reports 'Indonesia industrial automation market' at US$80.8 billion (2025) while Mordor Intelligence reports the 'Indonesia robotics market' at US$23.8 million (2025) — a difference of over 3,000x. These are not comparable: the first almost certainly includes all process control, instrumentation, electrical equipment and software across all industries including oil & gas and mining, while the second covers robot units only. Commercial market-sizing reports in this space are unreliable and were used only directionally. (3) INDONESIAN LAYOFF FIGURES — Kemnaker recorded 42,000+ layoffs January-June 2025 while KSPI claimed up to 70,000; government figures capture only formally reported terminations and systematically undercount. (4) MANUFACTURING SHARE OF GDP NARRATIVE — the Ministry of Industry argues Indonesia is NOT deindustrializing (citing 30 months of PMI expansion and 5.30% non-oil-gas manufacturing growth in 2025) while independent analysts point to the fall from ~32% of GDP (2002) to ~19% (2024) and mass factory closures; both are factually correct and describe different time horizons — growth in absolute output alongside structural decline in share. (5) INDONESIAN AVERAGE WAGE — one comparison source cites an Indonesian average gross salary of ~US$196/month against China's ~US$1,529/month; the Indonesian figure appears to understate actual formal-sector manufacturing wages (which cluster near or above UMP of ~IDR 3.32 million/month, ~US$205, but are higher in Jabodetabek industrial estates), so the ~7x gap should be read as an upper bound; the minimum-wage comparison (US$1.85 vs US$3.70/hour) is the more reliable one. (6) CHINA HUMANOID SHIPMENTS — 2025 figures for Unitree (~5,500) and AgiBot (~5,168) are company-disclosed and variously reported; 2026 targets (Unitree 20,000; AgiBot 40,000-50,000) are ambitions, not results, and China's overall humanoid market is widely suspected of inventory-channel stuffing to meet state deployment KPIs. (7) INDONESIA'S 25%-OF-GDP MANUFACTURING TARGET is quoted with both 2030 and 2035 deadlines in different Making Indonesia 4.0 materials.
